items.name: IncludeSelection
items.signature: { text : Str, lines : List(U64), problems : List(IncludeProblem) }
items.docs:
The lines an `include::` directive selects from its source, as returned
by [AsciiDoc.select_include].

- `text`: the selected lines after any `indent=`, joined with LF and with
  no final LF. As in include expansion, a CR that ends a line and a
  leading byte order mark are removed.
- `lines`: the one-based source line number of each selected line, in
  order. A final LF ends the last line rather than starting a new one,
  and an empty source has no lines, as in Asciidoctor.
- `problems`: each [AsciiDoc.IncludeProblem] found, once, in the order
  found. An empty list means the selection is clean.

```roc
expect AsciiDoc.select_include("one\ntwo\nthree\n", "lines=2..3", {}) == { text: "two\nthree", lines: [2, 3], problems: [] }
```
items.head: IncludeSelection

items.name: IncludeProblem
items.docs:
Something in an include's selection that Asciidoctor warns about, or
that it selects silently but is probably a mistake. Selection itself is
Asciidoctor's, so a strict caller rejects any problem and a lenient
caller ignores them.

Tag markers matter only when `tag=` or `tags=` selects and `lines=` is
absent. As in Asciidoctor, the open tags form a stack, which holds the
tags the selector names and, when it uses `*` or `!*`, every other tag
too. So does `!**` when the first other tag named is negated, as in
`!**;!x`. The first three problems are exactly Asciidoctor's warnings:

- `MissingTag(name)`: `tag=` or `tags=` requests `name` positively (not
  `*`, `**` or `!name`), but no `tag::name[]` marker opens it.
  Asciidoctor warns that the tag is not found.
- `UnclosedTag(name)`: `name` is still open when the source ends.
  Asciidoctor warns that it detected an unclosed tag. A re-opened tag
  nests, so `tag::x[]` twice needs `end::x[]` twice.
- `UnmatchedEnd(name)`: an `end::name[]` marker for a tag the selector
  names while `name` is not the innermost open tag. Asciidoctor warns of
  a mismatched end tag, which closes the innermost open `name` without
  changing what is selected, or of an unexpected one when `name` is not
  open. It ignores such an end silently for a tag that only a wildcard
  tracks, which may leave that tag unclosed.

Asciidoctor gives no warning for the other two:

- `InvalidLines(entry)`: an entry of `lines=`, without surrounding
  spaces, that is not `N`, `N..M` with N ≤ M, `N..` or `N..-1`, where N
  and M are plain decimal numbers and N is at least 1; or one whose first
  line is past the end of the source. Asciidoctor reads these entries
  without a warning: `4abc` selects line 4 and `+2` line 2, a reversed
  range such as `4..2` selects nothing (so a list of only reversed ranges
  selects every line), and a start of 0 or less selects nothing at all.
  A range that only partly runs past the end is not a problem.
- `EmptySelection`: no lines are selected, including from an empty
  source.

When `lines=` is present, `tag=` and `tags=` are ignored, as in
Asciidoctor, and report nothing.

```roc
expect AsciiDoc.select_include("a\n// tag::x[]\nb\n", "tag=x", {}).problems == [UnclosedTag("x")]
```
items.head: IncludeProblem

items.name: IncludeProps
items.docs:
Select the lines of `source` that an include directive with this
attribute list selects, such as `lines=1..4,indent=0` or `tag=example`.
`include::` expansion calls the same code, so a tool that expands
includes itself selects exactly the lines this package would. Both
select what Asciidoctor 2.0.23 selects.

The attributes it reads are `lines`, `tag`, `tags` and `indent`; others,
such as `leveloffset`, are ignored. The first of `lines=`, `tag=` and
`tags=` that is present wins, even with an empty value. An unquoted
`None` value leaves an attribute unset, and attribute references such
as `{range}` are not expanded.

- `lines=`: entries separated by `,`, or by `;` when there is no comma,
  each a line `N`, a range `N..M`, or an open range `N..` or `N..-1`.
  An empty `lines=` selects every line.
- `tag=` names one tag, even one containing `;` or `,`. `tags=` names
  several, separated like `lines=` entries. `!name` excludes a tag, `*`
  selects the lines inside any tag and `**` every line; the marker lines
  themselves are left out. Tags nest, and the innermost open tag decides
  whether a line is selected, so `tags=x;!y` selects `x` inside `y`. An
  empty `tag=` or `tag=!`, or a `tags=` naming no tag, selects every
  line and keeps the markers.
- A tag marker is the first `tag::NAME[]` or `end::NAME[]` on a line
  that starts a word and whose `[]` ends the line or is followed by a
  space. NAME has no whitespace. So `"tag::x[]"` in a string literal and
  `my_tag::x[]` are not markers.
- `indent=N`: finds the fewest leading whitespace characters on any
  nonempty selected line, counting a tab like a space, and removes that
  many from each nonempty line. It then indents each nonempty line by N
  spaces, and leaves empty lines empty. So with `indent=0`, a line
  indented by one tab and a line indented by two spaces each lose one
  character. An empty `indent=` dedents like `indent=0`, and a negative
  N changes nothing.

The source is read as Asciidoctor reads an included file that isn't
AsciiDoc: trailing whitespace is kept, so a line of only spaces counts
toward `indent=`, and the selected lines keep it wherever they land in
the document. When `include::` expansion includes an AsciiDoc file
(`.adoc`, `.asciidoc`, `.asc`, `.ad` or `.txt`), it first removes
trailing whitespace from each line, as Asciidoctor does. Tabs are not
expanded, as in a document that doesn't set `tabsize`. For a document
that does, supply the document's `tabsize` in props.

```roc
expect AsciiDoc.select_include("\t// tag::x[]\n\tfn = |x|\n\n\t\tx\n\t// end::x[]\n", "tag=x,indent=0", {}) == { text: "fn = |x|\n\n\tx", lines: [2, 3, 4], problems: [] }
```
The document an include directive is in, as far as selection depends
on it. `tabsize` is the document's `tabsize` attribute where the
directive appears, read as a number; 0, the default, expands no tabs.
Asciidoctor reads it from the document only, never from the
directive's own attribute list.
items.head: IncludeProps

items.name: select_include
items.docs:
Select included lines with document-specific tab expansion. With
`tabsize` set, `indent=` first expands each tab to the
next multiple of `tabsize` columns, counting each character before it
as one column, as `include::` expansion does in such a document. A tab
size above 1024 counts as 1024.

```roc
expect AsciiDoc.select_include("\t\tx\n\t  y", "indent=0", { tabsize: 4 }).text == "  x\ny"
```

items.name: CSV
items.docs:
RFC 4180-style CSV parsing and typed record decoding.

The dialect is RFC 4180 with the common relaxations of Python's `csv`
module (strict mode) and Rust's `csv` crate:

- Fields are separated by `,` and records by CRLF, LF or a lone CR. The line
  break after the last record is optional, and empty input has no records.
- A field is any run of bytes other than `,`, CR and LF, so fields may hold
  arbitrary UTF-8, tabs, spaces (kept verbatim) and control characters.
- A field that starts with `"` is quoted: it may contain `,`, CR and LF, a
  doubled `""` stands for one `"`, and the closing quote must be followed by
  `,`, a line break or the end of input. An unterminated quoted field is an
  error.
- A `"` anywhere else in an unquoted field is an ordinary character.
- A blank line is a record with one empty field, as RFC 4180's grammar says
  (Python's `csv.reader` returns an empty list for it instead).
- Rows may have different numbers of fields. A byte order mark is not
  removed; it is part of the first field.

Read a file as typed rows, text fields, or raw bytes:

- [CSV.decode_str] decodes rows into records whose field names match the header
  row, with the row type chosen by type inference;
- [CSV.rows_parser] runs a hand-built record parser (`record`, `field` and
  `Parser.keep`) over every row, matching columns by position;
- [CSV.parse_string_records] returns every field as a `Str`;
- [CSV.parse_str] returns the raw fields.

```roc
Person : { name : Str, age : U64 }

people : Try(List(Person), [InvalidCsv(CSV.Error)])
people = CSV.decode_str("name,age\nAda,36\nAlan,41\n", {})

expect people == Ok([{ name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "Alan", age: 41 }])
```

items.docs:
A dynamic JSON value and parser based on RFC 8259.

Use this module when a record type cannot describe a document: keys that
are not Roc identifiers (such as JSON-LD's `@context`), arrays whose
objects differ in shape, JSON Schema files, or data that must pass through
untouched. To decode JSON straight into your own record type, use the
builtin `Json` instead.

A `JsonValue` is one of:

- `Null`, `Bool` and `String`;
- `Number`, holding the exact number text from the input, so integers of any
  size and decimals of any precision survive unchanged. Convert it with
  [JsonValue.as_i64], [JsonValue.as_u64] or [JsonValue.as_dec];
- `Array`, and `Object`, whose members keep their source order.

[JsonValue.parse_str] is strict: it accepts exactly the JSON of RFC 8259
and rejects duplicate keys. [JsonValue.parse_str] takes [JsonValue.Props]
to accept common relaxations (comments, trailing commas, a byte order
mark, `NaN` and `Infinity`, lenient strings), to add checks (I-JSON
numbers, the top-level shape, size guards), and to choose what a repeated
key means. Nesting is limited to 128 levels by default.

[JsonValue.encode] writes a value back out as UTF-8 bytes containing
compact or indented JSON, refusing values that would not read back the same.

Strings and numbers read from the input share its bytes instead of being
copied, so a value keeps the whole input alive while any of them is.

```roc
expect {
    doc = JsonValue.parse_str("{\"@context\": \"https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-context.jsonld\", \"@graph\": []}", {})?
    doc.keys() == ["@context", "@graph"]
}
```

items.docs:
A Markdown document as a tree of blocks with inline content.

The parser follows [CommonMark 0.31.2](https://spec.commonmark.org/0.31.2/)
plus these GitHub Flavored Markdown extensions: tables, task list items,
strikethrough (`~~text~~`) and extended autolinks (`www.example.com`,
`https://example.com` and `me@example.com` without angle brackets). It also
accepts one extension of its own: a frontmatter block between two `---`
lines at the very start of a document, kept raw as `Frontmatter`.

Markdown has no syntax errors, so parsing never fails: [Markdown.parse_str]
returns `List(Markdown)` directly, and text that looks like broken syntax is
kept as text. Soft line breaks are kept as `"\n"` inside `Text`. Block
quotes and lists nest at most 1,000 levels deep, and so do emphasis,
strikethrough, links and images; deeper markers, delimiters and brackets
are read as text.

**Security:** raw HTML passes through unchanged as `HtmlBlock` and
`HtmlInline`, with no GFM tagfilter, and link destinations are not checked
(a `javascript:` URL is kept as written). If you render untrusted Markdown
to HTML, sanitize the HTML or drop those nodes and unsafe URLs yourself.

items.signature: { ordered : Bool, marker : U8, start : U64 }
items.docs:
Block structure follows the two-phase strategy of CommonMark 0.31.2
(appendix "A parsing strategy"): lines are consumed one at a time against a
stack of open blocks, then inline content is parsed once every link
reference definition is known. GFM tables and task list items are layered
on in the same places cmark-gfm hooks them in.

The first phase records what happens as a flat list of events (a container
opens or closes, a leaf block is complete, definitions were found), and the
tree is built from them afterwards. Only the innermost leaf block collects
lines while the document is read; they are kept outside the open-block
stack. That keeps the whole parse linear in the input: a list growing inside
a record that is itself stored elsewhere would be copied on every append.

items.name: Parser
items.docs:
Generic [parser combinators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parser_combinator)
for transforming input into structured values.

A `Parser(input, a, p)` is a value that describes how to read an `a` from the
front of an `input`. Combine small parsers with `keep`, `skip`, `map`,
`one_of`, `many` and `sep_by` to build larger ones, then run the result with
`parser.parse_str(source)` for text or `parser.parse(input)` for generic input.

This parser turns `"Game 1: 3 blue, 4 red; 1 red, 2 green, 6 blue; 2 green"`
into `{ id: 1, requirements: [[Blue(3), Red(4)], [Red(1), Green(2), Blue(6)], [Green(2)]] }`
using the shared UTF-8 primitives:
```roc
Requirement : [Green(U64), Red(U64), Blue(U64)]
RequirementSet : List(Requirement)
Game : { id : U64, requirements : List(RequirementSet) }

parse_game : Str -> Try(Game, [ParsingError])
parse_game = |s| {
    green = Parser.const(|x| Green(x)).keep(Parser.Utf8.digits({})).skip(Parser.Utf8.string(" green"))
    red = Parser.const(|x| Red(x)).keep(Parser.Utf8.digits({})).skip(Parser.Utf8.string(" red"))
    blue = Parser.const(|x| Blue(x)).keep(Parser.Utf8.digits({})).skip(Parser.Utf8.string(" blue"))

    requirement_set : Parser(_, RequirementSet, _)
    requirement_set = Parser.one_of([green, red, blue]).sep_by(Parser.Utf8.string(", "))

    requirements : Parser(_, List(RequirementSet), _)
    requirements = requirement_set.sep_by(Parser.Utf8.string("; "))

    game : Parser(_, Game, _)
    game =
        Parser.const(|id| |r| { id, requirements: r })
            .skip(Parser.Utf8.string("Game "))
            .keep(Parser.Utf8.digits({}))
            .skip(Parser.Utf8.string(": "))
            .keep(requirements)

    match game.parse_str(s) {
        Ok(g) => Ok(g)
        Err(ParseError(_)) => Err(ParsingError)
    }
}
```

Alternatives backtrack: when one alternative of `alt` or `one_of` fails, the
next one is tried on the original input, however much the failed one read.

Failures report the furthest position any parser reached. When a
repetition such as `many` stops at a bad element, or an alternative fails
after reading further than the one that succeeded, that failure is kept
and reported if the whole parse later fails at or before it.

The representation is internal and may change to improve efficiency or error problems.

items.name: codeunit_satisfies
items.docs:
Match one UTF-8 code unit when it satisfies the given predicate.

Fails on empty input or when the predicate returns `False`.

```roc
is_digit : U8 -> Bool
is_digit = |b| b >= '0' and b <= '9'

expect (Parser.Utf8.codeunit_satisfies(is_digit)).parse_str("0") == Ok('0')
expect (Parser.Utf8.codeunit_satisfies(is_digit)).parse_str("*").is_err()
```

items.name: codeunit
items.docs:
Match one exact UTF-8 code unit.

For a character outside ASCII, which is several code units, use `string`.

```roc
at_sign : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, [AtSign], _)
at_sign = Parser.const(AtSign).skip(Parser.Utf8.codeunit('@'))

expect at_sign.parse_str("@") == Ok(AtSign)
expect (at_sign).run_str("$").is_err()
```

items.name: utf8
items.docs: Match an exact sequence of UTF-8 bytes and return them.

items.name: string
items.docs:
Match the given `Str` exactly (case-sensitive) and return it.

```roc
expect (Parser.Utf8.string("Foo")).parse_str("Foo") == Ok("Foo")
expect (Parser.Utf8.string("Foo")).parse_str("Bar").is_err()
```

items.name: any_codeunit
items.docs:
Match any single `U8` code unit; fails only on empty input.

```roc
expect (Parser.Utf8.any_codeunit({})).parse_str("a") == Ok('a')
expect (Parser.Utf8.any_codeunit({})).parse_str("$") == Ok('$')
```

items.name: rest
items.docs:
Consume the rest of the input and return it as bytes; never fails.

```roc
expect {
    bytes = "consumes all the input".to_utf8()
    Parser.Utf8.rest({}).parse(bytes) == Ok(bytes)
}
```

items.name: rest_str
items.docs: Consume the rest of the input as a `Str`, failing if the bytes are not valid UTF-8.

items.name: digit
items.docs:
Parse one ASCII decimal digit into a `U64` from 0 through 9.

```roc
expect (Parser.Utf8.digit({})).parse_str("0") == Ok(0)
expect (Parser.Utf8.digit({})).parse_str("not a digit").is_err()
```

items.name: digits
items.docs:
Parse one or more ASCII decimal digits into a `U64`, accepting leading zeroes.

Fails when the input does not start with a digit or the value does not fit
in a `U64`. Signs and decimal points are not accepted.

```roc
expect (Parser.Utf8.digits({})).parse_str("0123") == Ok(123)
expect (Parser.Utf8.digits({})).parse_str("not a digit").is_err()
```

items.name: ByteClass
items.signature: { lo : U8x16, hi : U8x16, a : U8x16, b : U8x16, c : U8x16, members : List(Bool), kind : [Exact, Nibbles, Bytewise] }
items.docs:
A set of byte values, for finding or skipping runs of bytes 16 at a time.

Build a class once, outside any loop, and reuse it: construction derives
the lookup tables the vector scan uses. Any set of bytes works. A set
whose high-nibble rows have at most eight distinct shapes (every ASCII
class, and most practical ones) is scanned with two table lookups per 16
bytes; other sets fall back to a byte loop.

```roc
spaces = Parser.Utf8.ByteClass.from_bytes([' ', '\t'])
expect spaces.contains('\t')
expect !spaces.contains('x')
```
items.head: ByteClass

items.name: from_bytes
items.docs: The class holding exactly these bytes.

items.name: from_predicate
items.docs: The class holding every byte `b` for which `check(b)` is true.

items.name: complement
items.docs: The class holding every byte that is not in this one.

items.name: contains
items.docs: Whether the byte is in the class.

items.name: find_any
items.docs:
The index of the first byte at or after `pos` that is in `class`, or
the length of `bytes` if there is none. Scans 16 bytes at a time.

```roc
markup = Parser.Utf8.ByteClass.from_bytes(['<', '&'])
expect Parser.Utf8.find_any("a&b<c".to_utf8(), 0, markup) == 1
expect Parser.Utf8.find_any("abc".to_utf8(), 0, markup) == 3
```

items.name: skip_class
items.docs:
The index of the first byte at or after `pos` that is not in `class`,
or the length of `bytes` if every remaining byte is. Use it to skip a
run of name characters, digits or whitespace.

```roc
digits = Parser.Utf8.ByteClass.from_predicate(|b| b >= '0' and b <= '9')
expect Parser.Utf8.skip_class("123abc".to_utf8(), 0, digits) == 3
```

items.name: find_line_end
items.docs:
The index of the next `\n` or `\r` at or after `pos`, or the length of
`bytes` if there is none. Scans 16 bytes at a time.

```roc
expect Parser.Utf8.find_line_end("ab\r\ncd".to_utf8(), 0) == 2
```

items.name: span_class
items.docs:
Consume the longest run of bytes in `class`, possibly empty, and return
it as a slice of the input. It scans 16 bytes at a time, so prefer it to
`Parser.chomp_while` for runs longer than a few bytes.

```roc
name_char = Parser.Utf8.ByteClass.from_predicate(|b| (b >= 'a' and b <= 'z') or b == '-')
expect (Parser.Utf8.span_class(name_char)).run_str("foo-bar=1").map_ok(|r| r.rest) == Ok("=1")
```

items.name: ParseResult
items.docs:
The result of running a parser on part of an input: the parsed `value`
and the `rest` of the input, or a `ParseError` diagnostic. Generic
input positions use `InputOffset`; text runners supply `Text` coordinates.
items.head: ParseResult(input, a, p)

items.name: custom
items.signature: (input -> Try({ value : a, rest : input }, [ParseError(Diagnostic([..p]))])) -> Parser(input, a, p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Write a custom parser without using the provided combinators.

The function receives the remaining input and returns either the parsed
`value` with the `rest` it did not consume, or
`Err(ParseError({ problem, location, path }))`. Use `InputOffset(offset)`
for positions relative to this input, or preserve a native location and path.

items.name: run
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), input -> ParseResult(input, a, p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Run a parser on the start of an input, returning the parsed value and
the input it did not consume.

Most parsers consume part of `input` when they succeed. This allows you to string parsers
together that run one after the other. The part of the input that the first
parser did not consume, is used by the next parser.

On failure, the error is the furthest failure seen, with its `offset`
counted from the start of `input`. This is mostly useful when creating
your own parsing building blocks.

items.name: parse
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), input -> Try(a, [ParseError(Diagnostic(Parser.Problem(p)))]) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Run a parser on the given input, expecting it to consume all of it.

The input type only needs a `len` method, which is used both to detect
leftover input and to locate generic failures with `InputOffset` counted
from the start of `input`. Leftover input is a failure too: if some
parser failed at or beyond the leftover, its problem is reported;
otherwise the problem is `UnexpectedInput`. For text use
`parser.parse_str(source)`; byte lists use `parser.parse(bytes)`.

items.name: fail
items.signature: Parser.Problem(p) -> Parser(input, a, p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Parser that can never succeed, regardless of the given input.
It will always fail with the given error problem.

This is mostly useful as a 'base case' if all other parsers
in a `one_of` or `alt` have failed, to provide some more descriptive error problem.

items.name: const
items.docs:
Parser that will always produce the given `a`, without looking at the actual input.

This is the usual start of a pipeline: `const` supplies a (curried)
constructor function and each `keep` feeds it one parsed value.
```roc
parse_u32 : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, U32, _)
parse_u32 = Parser.const(U64.to_u32_wrap).keep(Parser.Utf8.digits({}))

expect parse_u32.parse_str("123") == Ok(123.U32)
```

items.name: alt
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, a, p) -> Parser(input, a, p)
items.docs:
Try the `first` parser and (only) if it fails, try the `second` parser as fallback.

The `second` parser starts from the same input as `first` (backtracking).
If both fail, the failure that reached further is reported; when both
stopped at the same place, the `second` one is.

items.name: one_of
items.signature: List(Parser(input, a, p)) -> Parser(input, a, p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Try a list of parsers in turn, until one of them succeeds.

Each parser starts from the same input. An empty list always fails.
For UTF-8 input, [Parser.one_of] behaves the same way.
```roc
color : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, [Red, Green, Blue], _)
color =
    Parser.one_of([
        Parser.const(Red).skip(Parser.Utf8.string("red")),
        Parser.const(Green).skip(Parser.Utf8.string("green")),
        Parser.const(Blue).skip(Parser.Utf8.string("blue")),
    ])

expect color.parse_str("green") == Ok(Green)
```

items.name: map_problem
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), (Parser.Problem(p) -> Parser.Problem(q)) -> Parser(input, a, q)
items.docs:
Translate structured problems while preserving the furthest failure.
Wrap a closed native union in a domain tag when combining formats.

items.name: map
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), (a -> b) -> Parser(input, b, p)
items.docs:
Transforms the result of parsing into something else,
using the given transformation function.

items.name: map2
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, b, p), (a, b -> c) -> Parser(input, c, p)
items.docs:
Transforms the result of parsing into something else,
using the given two-parameter transformation function.

items.name: map3
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, b, p), Parser(input, c, p), (a, b, c -> d) -> Parser(input, d, p)
items.docs:
Transforms the result of parsing into something else,
using the given three-parameter transformation function.

If you need transformations with more inputs,
take a look at `keep`.

items.name: flatten
items.signature: Parser(input, Try(a, Parser.Problem(p)), p) -> Parser(input, a, p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Removes a layer of `Try` from running the parser.

Use this to map functions that return a `Try` over the parser:
an `Err(msg)` value becomes a failure with that problem, reported where
the inner parser started.

```roc
even : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, U64, _)
even =
    Parser.Utf8.digits({})
        .map(|n| if n % 2 == 0 { Ok(n) } else { Err(OddNumber) })
        .flatten()

expect even.parse_str("42") == Ok(42)
expect even.parse_str("7") == Err(ParseError(Parser.Diagnostic.{ problem: OddNumber, location: Text({ offset: 0, line: 1, column: 1 }), path: [] }))
```

items.name: and_then
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), (a -> Parser(input, b, p)) -> Parser(input, b, p)
items.docs:
Run `first`, then build the next parser from its value and run that.

Use this when what comes next depends on what was read, such as a
length prefix. When the next parser is fixed, prefer `keep`, `skip`
and `map`, which are simpler and let the parser be built once.

```roc
sized : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, List(U8), _)
sized = Parser.Utf8.digit({}).and_then(|n| Parser.Utf8.any_codeunit({}).many().map(|bytes| bytes.take_first(n)))
```

items.name: lazy
items.signature: ({} -> Parser(input, a, p)) -> Parser(input, a, p)
items.docs:
Runs a parser lazily.

This is (only) useful when dealing with a recursive structure.
For instance, consider a type `Comment : { message : Str, responses : List(Comment) }`.
Without `lazy`, you would ask the compiler to build an infinitely deep parser.
(Resulting in a compiler error.)

A top-level parser that refers to itself has to be a function, called
inside `lazy`: `tree = |{}| ...` with `Parser.lazy(|_| tree({}))`. Top-level
parsers that refer to each other need one `lazy` somewhere in the cycle,
so that each value can be built before the other is used.

items.name: maybe
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p) -> Parser(input, Try(a, [Missing]), p)
items.docs:
Make a parser optional.

Returns `Ok(value)` when the given parser succeeds, and `Err(Missing)`
without consuming input when it fails, so the result never fails.

items.name: many
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p) -> Parser(input, List(a), p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
A parser which runs the element parser *zero* or more times on the input,
returning a list containing all the parsed elements.

Repetition stops at the first element that fails, or that succeeds
without consuming any input; that element's value is not included.
(Without this rule, a parser such as `chomp_while` or `maybe(p)` that can
succeed on empty input would repeat forever.) The failure of the element
that stopped the repetition is kept, so if the parse later fails there,
that failure is what gets reported.

items.name: one_or_more
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p) -> Parser(input, List(a), p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
A parser which runs the element parser *one* or more times on the input,
returning a list containing all the parsed elements.

Fails when the first element fails. Also see [Parser.many].

items.name: between
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, open, p), Parser(input, close, p) -> Parser(input, a, p)
items.docs:
Runs a parser for an 'opening' delimiter, then your main parser, then the 'closing' delimiter,
and only returns the result of your main parser.

Useful to recognize structures surrounded by delimiters (like braces, parentheses, quotes, etc.)

```roc
between_brackets = |parser| parser.between(Parser.Utf8.codeunit('['), Parser.Utf8.codeunit(']'))
```

items.name: sep_by_one_or_more
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, sep, p) -> Parser(input, List(a), p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Parse one or more values separated by `separator`.
The separators are consumed and omitted from the result.

A trailing separator that is not followed by a value is left unconsumed.

items.name: sep_by
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, sep, p) -> Parser(input, List(a), p) where [input.len : input -> U64]
items.docs:
Parse zero or more values separated by `separator`.
The separators are consumed and omitted from the result.

```roc
parse_numbers : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, List(U64), _)
parse_numbers = Parser.Utf8.digits({}).sep_by(Parser.Utf8.codeunit(','))

expect parse_numbers.parse_str("1,2,3") == Ok([1, 2, 3])
```

items.name: ignore
items.docs:
Discard a parser's value while preserving how much input it consumes.

Useful with `many` to skip a repeated token without collecting values.

items.name: keep
items.signature: Parser(input, (a -> b), p), Parser(input, a, p) -> Parser(input, b, p)
items.docs:
Run a parser producing a function, then a parser producing its argument,
and return the function result.

Start with `const(|a| |b| ...)` and add one `keep` per argument, as in
the module example. The function must be curried (`|a| |b| ...`, not
`|a, b| ...`), because its arguments are applied one at a time.

items.name: skip
items.signature: Parser(input, a, p), Parser(input, _, p) -> Parser(input, a, p)
items.docs:
Run two parsers in sequence, discarding the second parser's value.

Both parsers must succeed, and the input read by the second is consumed.
```roc
at_sign : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, [AtSign], _)
at_sign = Parser.const(AtSign).skip(Parser.Utf8.codeunit('@'))

expect at_sign.parse_str("@") == Ok(AtSign)
```

items.name: chomp_until
items.signature: a -> Parser(List(a), List(a), p) where [a.is_eq : a, a -> Bool]
items.docs:
Match zero or more codeunits until it reaches the given codeunit.
The given codeunit is not included in the match and is not consumed.
Fails if the codeunit never appears in the remaining input.

This can be used with [Parser.skip] to ignore text.

```roc
ignore_text : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, U64, _)
ignore_text =
    Parser.const(|d| d)
        .skip(Parser.chomp_until(':'))
        .skip(Parser.Utf8.codeunit(':'))
        .keep(Parser.Utf8.digits({}))

expect ignore_text.parse_str("ignore preceding text:123") == Ok(123)
```

This can be used with [Parser.keep] to capture a list of `U8` codeunits.

```roc
capture_text : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, List(U8), _)
capture_text =
    Parser.const(|codeunits| codeunits)
        .keep(Parser.chomp_until(':'))
        .skip(Parser.Utf8.codeunit(':'))

expect capture_text.parse_str("Roc:") == Ok(['R', 'o', 'c'])
```

Use [Str.from_utf8_lossy] to turn the results into a `Str`.

Also see [Parser.chomp_while].

items.name: chomp_while
items.docs:
Match zero or more codeunits until the check returns false.
The codeunit that returned false is not included in the match.
Note: a `chomp_while` parser always succeeds, possibly consuming nothing.

This can be used with [Parser.skip] to ignore text.
This is useful for chomping whitespace or variable names.

```roc
ignore_numbers : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, Str, _)
ignore_numbers =
    Parser.const(|str| str)
        .skip(Parser.chomp_while(|b| b >= '0' and b <= '9'))
        .keep(Parser.Utf8.string("TEXT"))

expect ignore_numbers.parse_str("0123456789876543210TEXT") == Ok("TEXT")
```

This can be used with [Parser.keep] to capture a list of `U8` codeunits.

```roc
capture_numbers : Parser(Parser.Utf8.Bytes, List(U8), _)
capture_numbers =
    Parser.const(|codeunits| codeunits)
        .keep(Parser.chomp_while(|b| b >= '0' and b <= '9'))
        .skip(Parser.Utf8.string("TEXT"))

expect capture_numbers.parse_str("123TEXT") == Ok(['1', '2', '3'])
```

Use [Str.from_utf8_lossy] to turn the results into a `Str`.

Also see [Parser.chomp_until].

items.name: span
items.signature: Parser(List(item), a, p) -> Parser(List(item), List(item), p)
items.docs:
Run a parser and return the input it consumed, instead of its value.

The result is a slice of the input, not a copy, so recognising a token
with small parsers and keeping its text costs no allocation.

```roc
identifier = Parser.span(Parser.Utf8.codeunit('$').skip(Parser.chomp_while(|b| b >= 'a' and b <= 'z')))
expect identifier.parse_str("$abc") == Ok("$abc".to_utf8())
```

items.docs:
Lossless parsing of Roc source into tokens, syntax trees and diagnostics.
Byte spans are half-open. Comments and whitespace are tokens.

Expressions include interpolated and multiline strings, typed literals,
calls, field access, operators, pipes, nominal construction and control flow.
Binding patterns, type declarations, annotations, constraints, imports and
module, app, package and platform headers retain their syntax structure.
Parsing does not resolve names or establish that a program typechecks.

Parsing retains the source once and appends nodes and children to flat lists
that each parser receives and returns directly, so they stay uniquely owned.
Nesting is bounded at 128; documents over 1,048,576 tokens retain all tokens but
skip syntax construction with `Limited` status. Malformed input returns a
partial tree and diagnostics, including arbitrary non-UTF-8 source bytes.

[RocSyntax.validate] and quoted `RocSyntax` values require complete file syntax
without recovery diagnostics. Validation also rejects `...` placeholder
expressions by default; strings and comments containing `...` are ordinary
source text. This checks syntax, not name resolution or type correctness.

items.name: XmlCore
items.docs:
XML document tree and parser based on the XML 1.0 (Fifth Edition)
specification.

The parser checks well-formedness for documents without a document type
declaration. It supports an optional XML declaration, nested elements,
attributes, character data, CDATA sections, the five predefined entity
references (`<` `>` `&` `'` `"`), and decimal and
hexadecimal character references. Comments and processing instructions are
checked and then dropped from the tree.

The tree is normalised the way an XML processor reports it: line endings
become `\n` (XML 1.0 section 2.11), attribute values are normalised as
CDATA attributes (section 3.3.3), references are replaced by their text,
and adjacent character data (including CDATA sections and text on both
sides of a comment) is merged into one `Text` node.

Document type declarations (`<!DOCTYPE ...>`) are rejected, so entities
other than the predefined ones are never declared and referring to one is
a well-formedness error. Namespaces are not processed: a name such as
`svg:path` is kept as written; [Xml.Namespaced] resolves them. Input is already
decoded text, so a declared encoding is reported but not used to decode.

Read a document with `Xml.parse_str(source, props)`, selecting explicit
resource limits for untrusted input, then walk it with pattern matching or [Xml.Node]
helpers `name`, `attribute`, `children_named` and `text`. [Xml.reader]
reads a document one event at a time instead:

```roc
expect {
    xml = Xml.parse_str("<feed><title>News</title><link href='/a'/></feed>", {})?
    titles = xml.root.children_named("title").map(|title| title.text())
    links = xml.root.children_named("link").map(|link| link.attribute("href"))
    titles == ["News"] and links == [Ok("/a")]
}
```

Originally written by [Johannes Maas](https://github.com/j-maas).

items.name: XmlNsCore
items.docs:
XML with namespaces resolved, following
[Namespaces in XML 1.0 (Third Edition)](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml-names/).

Every element and attribute name is split into an optional prefix and a
local part, and the prefix is resolved to the namespace bound to it in
scope. A binding (an `xmlns` or `xmlns:p` attribute) covers its element
and that element's descendants, and an inner binding shadows an outer
one. Unprefixed elements are in the default namespace, if one is in
scope; unprefixed attributes are in no namespace. The `xml` prefix is
always bound to [Xml.Namespaced.xml_namespace].

Names are resolved while the document is read, so only one tree is ever
built. Declarations are kept in each element's `bindings`, in source
order, and every name keeps its prefix, so a tree can be written back
with the prefixes and declarations it was read with.

```roc
expect {
    doc = Xml.Namespaced.parse_str("<feed xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom'><title>News</title></feed>", {})?
    atom = Uri("http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom")
    doc.root.children_named(atom, "title").map(|title| title.text()) == ["News"]
}
```

Namespace names are compared as strings, as the specification requires,
and a namespace problem is reported with the location of the start tag.
Problems are reported in document order: a namespace problem in a start
tag comes before a well-formedness error later in the document.

A rule of Namespaces in XML 1.0 that a document breaks.

- `UndeclaredPrefix(p)`: an element or attribute name uses a prefix
  with no binding in scope.
- `ReservedPrefix(p)`: `xmlns` is declared or used as an element
  prefix, or `xml` is bound to a namespace other than its own.
- `ReservedNamespace(u)`: the `xml` or `xmlns` namespace is bound to
  another prefix or as the default.
- `EmptyNamespace(p)`: `xmlns:p=""`, which XML 1.0 does not allow.
- `NotAQName(name)`: more than one colon, or an empty or malformed
  prefix or local part.
- `DuplicateAttribute(name)`: two attributes with the same namespace and
  local name, such as `a:x` and `b:x` with `a` and `b` bound to the
  same namespace.

items.name: WriteProps
items.docs:
How [Xml.Namespaced.encode] writes a document.

- `declaration`: `Plain` writes `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>`
  and a line feed, `Standalone` also declares `standalone="yes"`, and
  `Omitted` writes no declaration.
- `prefixes`: `AsRead` writes each element's own `bindings` and each
  name's own prefix. `Table(entries)` writes each name with its
  namespace's prefix from the table, ignoring the tree's prefixes and
  bindings, and declares on the root, in table order, every namespace
  the document uses. An empty prefix makes a namespace the default for
  elements, declared with `xmlns="u"` on the first element that needs it
  (the root, when it is in that namespace), and `xmlns=""` or `xmlns="u"`
  is written wherever the default must change. The `xml` namespace is
  always written with `xml`.
- `attribute_order`: `AsGiven` keeps each element's attributes in order,
  and `SortedBy(compare)` sorts them.

items.name: EncodeProblem
items.docs:
Why a tree cannot be written as namespace-well-formed XML 1.0.

- `InvalidName(name)`: a prefix or local name that is not an NCName, or
  a binding of a reserved prefix, a table that gives one prefix two
  namespaces, or `Prefix(p)` bound to `NoNamespace`.
- `InvalidChar(code)`: a character XML 1.0 does not allow.
- `UnboundNamespace(namespace)`: a name whose prefix is not bound to its
  namespace where it is used, or a namespace missing from the table.
  `""` stands for no namespace, when a default namespace is in scope.
- `DuplicateAttribute(name)`: two attributes with the same namespace
  and local name.

items.name: encode
items.docs: Encode a document as XML 1.0 UTF-8 bytes. The output is a function of the tree and `props` alone, and [Xml.Namespaced.parse_str] reads it back as the same tree, up to prefixes and bindings with `Table`. Text escapes `&` and `<`, `>` after `]]`, and a carriage return as ` `. Attribute values are double-quoted and also escape `"`, tab and line feed, so they survive attribute value normalisation. A failure names the problem and the path of written element names from the root to the element it is in. ```roc expect { doc = Xml.Namespaced.parse_str("x < y", {})? doc.encode({ declaration: Omitted }).map_ok(|bytes| Str.from_utf8(bytes) ?? crash "XML encoding produced invalid UTF-8") == Ok("x < y") } expect { doc = Xml.Namespaced.parse_str("", {})? doc.encode({ declaration: Standalone, prefixes: Table([{ prefix: "w", namespace: "urn:w" }]) }).map_ok(|bytes| Str.from_utf8(bytes) ?? crash "XML encoding produced invalid UTF-8") == Ok("\n") } ```

	Float(F64),

items.docs:
A practical YAML configuration parser.

This module implements a YAML 1.2 subset aimed at configuration files and
Markdown frontmatter. It supports a single document (optionally between
`---` and `...` markers), block mappings and sequences (including compact and
indentless sequences), single-line flow collections, comments, literal and
folded block scalars, single-line quoted scalars with all YAML escapes, and
plain scalars resolved with the YAML 1.2 core schema (null, booleans, decimal,
octal and hexadecimal integers, floats, `.inf` and `.nan`).

Mapping keys are their source text, so `1` and `01` are different keys.
Nesting is limited to 100 levels. Anchors, aliases, tags, directives,
complex keys, multi-line flow collections, multi-line quoted or plain
scalars, and multi-document streams are rejected with a parse error rather
than misread.

For source-preserving syntax highlighting, [Yaml.tokenize_str] and
[Yaml.tokenize_bytes] return original byte spans and diagnostics even for
incomplete snippets. [Yaml.highlight_category] provides theme categories.

There are two ways to read a document:

- [Yaml.decode_str] reads it straight into your own record, list, dict or tuple
  type, which the compiler infers from how the result is used;
- [Yaml.parse_str] returns a `Yaml` tree, which [Yaml.get], [Yaml.at],
  [Yaml.get_path] and the `as_` helpers make easy to explore.

A `Yaml` tree value is one of:

- `Null` for `null`, `~`, an empty value or an empty document;
- `Bool`, `Int` (an `I64`; larger integers are an error) and `Float` for
  plain scalars the core schema resolves;
- `Text` for quoted scalars, block scalars and any other plain scalar;
- `Sequence` and `Mapping` for collections. Mapping entries keep their source
  order, and a duplicate key is an error.

items.docs:
Parse one YAML configuration document from a string.

Empty input produces `Null`. Invalid input returns `InvalidYaml` with a
one-based line and column. See the module description for the supported subset.

```roc
expect Yaml.parse_str("draft: false", {}) == Ok(Mapping([{ key: "draft", value: Bool(False) }]))
```

items.name: parser
items.docs:
A [Parser] that reads the rest of its input as one YAML document, for
composing YAML with other parsers.

It always consumes all input. `ParseError` carries the native YAML problem
and the shared location/path envelope; text runners provide original text coordinates.

```roc
expect (Yaml.parser({})).parse_str("a: 1") == Ok(Mapping([{ key: "a", value: Int(1) }]))
```

items.name: get
items.docs:
The value stored under `key` in a mapping. Anything else, or a mapping
without that key, is `Err(Missing)`.

```roc
expect Yaml.parse_str("title: Post", {}).map_ok(|doc| doc.get("title")) == Ok(Ok(Text("Post")))
```

items.name: at
items.docs:
The item at a zero-based `index` of a sequence. Anything else, or an
index past the end, is `Err(Missing)`.

```roc
expect Yaml.parse_str("[a, b]", {}).map_ok(|doc| doc.at(1)) == Ok(Ok(Text("b")))
```

items.name: get_path
items.docs:
Follow a path of mapping keys and sequence indexes. A segment applied
to a sequence must be a decimal index such as `"0"`.

```roc
expect {
    doc = Yaml.parse_str("jobs:\n  build:\n    steps: [checkout, test]\n", {})?
    doc.get_path(["jobs", "build", "steps", "1"]) == Ok(Text("test"))
}
```

booleans, are `Err(WrongType)`; use [Yaml.decode_str] to read a plain

items.name: to_inspect
items.docs:
Render a parsed YAML value in Roc source-like notation for inspection.

The output is meant for debugging and test messages, not for writing
YAML. Control characters in text and keys are escaped, so the output is
always printable on one line.

```roc
expect Yaml.to_inspect(Sequence([Int(1), Text("a")])) == "Sequence([Int(1), Text(\"a\")])"
```

items.name: decode_str
items.docs:
Decode one YAML document straight into a Roc type, chosen by type
inference.

- A mapping decodes into a record (by field name), or a `Dict` with
  `Str` or integer keys. Unknown keys are skipped; use [Yaml.decode_str]
  with `unknown_keys: Reject` to make them an error.
- A sequence decodes into a `List` or, when it has exactly the right
  number of items, a tuple.
- A scalar is resolved for the type that asks for it, using the YAML 1.2
  core schema: `Str` takes any quoted or block scalar and any plain
  scalar except a null, so `version: 1.10` stays `"1.10"`; `Bool`, the
  integer types, `F32`, `F64` and `Dec` take the matching core-schema
  forms; a tag union without payloads takes the tag's name.
- A null (`null`, `~` or an empty value) decodes as an empty list,
  dict or record, and fills a `Try(_, [Null])` field with `Err(Null)`.
- A `Try(_, [Missing])` field is `Err(Missing)` when its key is absent.
  Any other absent field fails with `InvalidYaml`, whose problem is
  `MissingRequiredField(name)` and whose path identifies that key.

Invalid YAML and values that do not fit the type both fail with
`InvalidYaml`, at the line and column of the offending value.

```roc
Config : { name : Str, version : Str, port : U16, debug : Try(Bool, [Missing]) }

expect {
    config : Try(Config, [InvalidYaml(Yaml.Error)])
    config = Yaml.decode_str("name: app\nversion: 1.10\nport: 8080\n", {})
    config == Ok({ name: "app", version: "1.10", port: 8080, debug: Err(Missing) })
}
```
